name: GO Classes Test Series 2024 | Theory of Computation | Test 3

question.text:
Consider the following languages :

  1. The language of the $\text{CFG}$ with productions $\text{S} \rightarrow \text{AS}\mid \text{SB}\mid \epsilon, \text{A} \rightarrow 0$, and $\text{B} \rightarrow 1$
  2. The language of regular expression $0^{\ast} 1^{\ast}$

Which of the following is true ?

  1. $1$ is proper subset of $2$
  2. $2$ is proper subset of $1$
  3. $1=2$
  4. Neither $1$ is subset of $2$, nor $2$ is subset of $1$.

Consider the following language $\mathrm{L}$ with the alphabet $\{0,1\}$. The empty string is not in $\mathrm{L}.$ If the string is nonempty and has even length, then it is in $\mathrm{L}.$ If the string has odd length, then it is in $\mathrm{L}$ if and only if it is a palindrome.

Which of the following best describes $\mathrm{L}?$

  1. Regular
  2. DCFL but not regular
  3. CFL but not DCFL
  4. Not CFL

Consider the following languages:

  1. The language (accepted by final state) of $\operatorname{PDA}(\{p, q\},\{0,1\},\{\text{X, Z}\}, \delta, q, \text{Z},\{p\})$ with $\delta$ defined by the rules $\delta(q, 0, \text{Z})=\{(q, \text{X Z)}\}, \delta(q, 0, X)=\{(q, \text{X X)}\}, \delta(q, 1, \text{X})= \{(p, \epsilon)\}$, and $\delta(p, 1, \text{X})=\{(p, \epsilon)\}$.
  2. The language of the CFG with productions $\text{S} \rightarrow 0\; \text{S}\; 1\mid 0 \;\text{S}\mid \epsilon$.

Which of the following is true ?

  1. $1$ is proper subset of $2$
  2. $2$ is proper subset of $1$
  3. $1 = 2$
  4. Neither $1$ is subset of $2$, nor $2$ is subset of $1$

Which of the following statements are true?

  1. The grammar, $\mathrm{G}: \mathrm{E} \rightarrow \mathrm{E}+\mathrm{E}\mid \mathrm{E} \ast \mathrm{E} \mid x$ is ambiguous.
  2. A regular grammar can never be ambiguous.
  3. A grammar is ambiguous if there is some string $w$ such that $w's$ right-most derivation differs from its left-most derivation.
  4. A grammar is ambiguous if there is some string w such that w has two different parse trees.

$$ \begin{aligned}
&\mathrm{S} \rightarrow \mathrm{A0B}\\
&\mathrm{A} \rightarrow \mathrm{BB} \mid 0\\
&\mathrm{B} \rightarrow \mathrm{AA} \mid 1
\end{aligned} $$
What is the number of terminal strings of length $5$ generated by the context-free grammar shown above?

Which of the following languages is/are Context Free(CFL)?

  1. $\left\{w \# w^{\prime} \mid w, w^{\prime} \in \{a,b\}^{\ast }\right.$ and $\left.w \neq w^{\prime}\right\}$.
  2. $\left\{0^{n} 1^{m} \mid n \leq m \leq 2 n\right\}$.
  3. $a^{\ast } b^{\ast } c^{\ast }-\left\{a^{n} b^{n} c^{n} \mid n \geq 0\right\}$.
  4. $\left\{w \in\{0,1,2\}^{\ast } \mid \#_{0}(w)=\#_{1}(w)=\#_{2}(w)\right\}$

A grammar is said to be "useless" if and only if it produces no terminal strings. If $\text{S}$ is the start symbol, which of the following grammars is (are) "useless"?

  1. $\begin{aligned}&\text{S} \rightarrow \text{AB} \mid \text{AS}\\ &\text{A} \rightarrow \text{B} \mid a\\ &\text{B} \rightarrow \text{A} \mid b \end{aligned}$

 

  1. $\begin{aligned} &\text{S} \rightarrow \text{SA}\mid \text{AS}\mid \text{SB}\\ &\text{A} \rightarrow a\\ &\text{B} \rightarrow a \mid b \end{aligned}$

 

  1. $\begin{aligned} &\text{S} \rightarrow \epsilon \mid \text{A} \\ &\text{A} \rightarrow \text{B} \\&\text{B} \rightarrow \text{C} \\&\text{C} \rightarrow a \end{aligned}$

 

  1. None
  2. Only II
  3. Only III
  4. Only II, III

Which of the following languages are not context free?

  1. $\text{L}_{1}=\left\{0^{n} 1^{2 n} \mid n \geq 0\right\}$
  2. $\text{L}_{2}=\left\{w \in\{0,1\}^{\ast} \mid w \neq w^{\text{R}}\right\}$.
  3. $\text{L}_{3}=\left\{w w w \mid w \in\{0,1\}^{\ast}\right\}$.
  4. $\text{L}_{4}=\left\{x / y / z \mid x, y, z \in\{0,1\}^{\ast}\right.$ are binary numbers such that $\left.x+y=z\right\}$. The alphabet for this language is $\{0,1, /\}$. For example, $10 / 10 / 100 \in \text{L}_{3}$ and $11 / 1 / 001 \notin \text{L}_{3}$.

Which of the following languages are $\text{CFL}$ But Not Regular?

  1. $\mathrm{L}=\left\{a^{2 n} b^{3 n} \mid \mathrm{n}>0\right\}$
  2. $\mathrm{L}=\left\{a^{2 n} b^{3 m} \mid \mathrm{m}, \mathrm{n}>0\right\}$
  3. $\mathrm{L}=\left\{a^{2 n} b^{3} \mid \mathrm{n}>0\right\}$
  4. $\mathrm{L}=\left\{a^{2 n} b^{n+m} \mid \mathrm{n}, \mathrm{m}>0\right\}$

Consider the following Grammar:
$$\mathrm{S} \rightarrow r l \mid r \text{S} l \mid \mathrm{S S}$$
Which of the following strings can be generated by this grammar?

  1. $rrllrl$
  2. $rllrrrll$
  3. $rrlrl\; rllrl\; rrl$
  4. $rrrll\; lrlr\; rll$

Let $\mathrm{L}=\left\{a^{p} \mid p\; \text{is prime} \right\}$ be a language. Which of the following are true?

  1. $\mathrm{L}$ is Not context free language.
  2. $\mathrm{L}^{\ast}$ is Not Context free language.
  3. Complement of $\text{L}^{\ast}$ is regular.
  4. Complement of $\mathrm{L}$ is $\text{CFL}.$

Consider the following languages :

  1. $\text{L}_{1}=\left\{w w \mid w \in\{a\}^{\ast}\right\}$
  2. $\text{L}_{2}=\left\{w w \mid w \in\{a, b\}^{\ast}\right\}$

Which of the above languages is Non-regular But CFL?

  1. Only $\text{L}_{1}$
  2. Only $\text{L}_{2}$
  3. Both
  4. None

A context-free grammar has a set of terminals $\{0,1,-\}$, a set of non-terminals $\{\mathrm{N}, \mathrm{P}\}$, where $\mathrm{N}$ is the start symbol, and productions given by the following .
$$
\begin{aligned}
&\mathrm{N} \rightarrow 0 \mid \mathrm{P} \mid -\;\mathrm{P} \\
&\mathrm{P} \rightarrow 1 \mid \mathrm{P}\; 0 \mid \mathrm{P} \;1
\end{aligned}
$$
What can be said about the language generated by this grammar?

  1. It is regular.
  2. It is Non-regular But DCFL.
  3. It is non-DCFL but CFL.
  4. It is Non-CFL.

Every day, a weather station records whether the day was sunny $\text{(S),}$ cloudy $\text{(C)}$ or rainy $\text{(R)}.$ A sequence of records over several days is a string in $\{\mathrm{S}, \mathrm{C}, \mathrm{R}\}^{\ast}$. We call a sequence of records $\mathrm{GO}$-like if:

  • There are never more than three consecutive rainy days, and
  • There are never more than five consecutive non-sunny days.

The language of $\text{GO}$-like sequences is

  1. Regular
  2. DCFL but Not regular
  3. CFL but not DCFL
  4. Not CFL

An infinite language is $\text{REG-immune}$ if it contains no infinite subset that is a regular language.

Which of the following are $\text{REG-immune}$ languages?

  1. $\left\{a^{n} b^{n} \mid n \geq 0\right\}$
  2. $\left\{w w \mid w \in(a+b)^{\ast }\right\}$
  3. $\left\{w \# w \mid w \in(a+b)^{\ast }\right\}$
  4. $\left\{a^{p} \mid p\;\text {is prime} \right\}$
